segments.title: What would let Australia and New Zealand survive Washington?
segments.body: The patron's question asks what would have to change about HMAS Australia and HMS New Zealand for Britain to fight for their retention at Washington. The proposed answer begins with delaying their orders until an enlarged Tiger design with 15-inch guns becomes a plausible choice. Better wartime performance and a demonstrated need for commerce protection would give those ships a stronger retention case than the historical Indefatigables. A separate battlecruiser category, with Dominion entitlements, would then provide a treaty framework for keeping them. Each stage is part of an alternate history, and the diplomatic compromise remains conditional.

evidence.note: The opening patron question asks what would have to differ about Australia and New Zealand for Britain to fight for their retention at Washington.
A procurement delay and enlarged Tiger-derived 15-inch-gun ships are proposed.
A separate battlecruiser treaty category and Dominion entitlements provide the proposed retention framework.
The conclusion requires demonstrated wartime value and 15-inch-gun ships to justify retention.

segments.question: What would have to be different about HMAS Australia and HMS New Zealand to justify Britain fighting for their retention at Washington?
segments.answerShort: Their orders would need to be delayed until they could be built as 15-inch-gun Tiger derivatives, their wartime service would need to demonstrate their value, and Washington would need a separate battlecruiser category with Dominion entitlements.

segments.title: Imperial fleet units were designed for commerce protection
segments.body: The 1909 plan would give Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and other parts of the empire more responsibility for their own sea lanes. A battlecruiser formed the heavy element of a mixed force built for convoy escort, deterrence, and hunting surface raiders such as Vice-Admiral von Spee's East Asia Squadron. New Zealand was prepared to fund and support the China Station formation, but it did not want to supply a wholly New Zealand crew because of its population size. That arrangement produced HMS New Zealand, while Australia operated HMAS Australia. These commerce-protection units could oblige an opponent to send substantial forces to deal with them. They were too small to fight a concentrated enemy navy.

evidence.note: The 1909 fleet-unit composition, New Zealand funding and crewing distinction, commerce-protection roles, and limits of deterrence against concentrated forces are explained.

segments.summary: The 1909 Imperial Conference scheme paired a battlecruiser with cruisers, destroyers, and submarines for trade protection, convoy escort, deterrence, and raider hunting.

segments.title: Canada's stop-start fleet policy slows the 1909 scheme
segments.body: Canada repeatedly reopened its naval options while Australia and New Zealand moved quickly on the 1909 fleet-unit scheme. Its policy could swing between minimal armament and a proposal for three Queen Elizabeth-class battleships. That hesitation supplies the slower procurement timetable needed for the alternate scenario. It also shows how Canada could leap from delay to an unusually large capital-ship proposal instead of building its fleet incrementally.

evidence.note: Comparison of Canada's repeated reconsideration and three-Queen-Elizabeth proposal with the rapid Australian and New Zealand decisions.

segments.summary: Canada repeatedly revisits its naval commitment and at one point considers three Queen Elizabeth-class battleships, while Australia and New Zealand place their orders quickly.

segments.title: Lord Dudley drives Australia's rapid naval procurement
segments.body: William Ward, second Earl of Dudley, supplied much of the political drive behind Australia's unusually fast decision. He drew lessons from the Russo-Japanese and Spanish-American wars, especially the exposure created by Australia's coastal population and weak internal communications. His answer was to strengthen local ships and infrastructure before asking the Royal Navy for more support. He wanted the whole fleet unit, including submarines, destroyers, and a battlecruiser, and his momentum helped pull New Zealand into the scheme. His attempt to place an order immediately after the conference still required approval. Dudley then pressed Australian politicians, British industry, the Admiralty, the Treasury, and the Foreign Office to complete the order in December 1909.

evidence.note: Dudley's strategic reasoning and the speed with which he drove the Australian and British systems are described.

segments.summary: Governor-General Lord Dudley turns the 1909 conference concept into an unusually rapid Australian order and helps pull New Zealand into the scheme.

segments.title: Dudley's political weakness makes a procurement delay plausible
segments.body: Dudley's record in Australia also exposed the limits of his methods. His strained relationship with Labor leader Andrew Fisher made it risky for a governor-general to appear aligned against a major party. Fisher's frugality and socialist background sat uneasily with Dudley's attachment to vice-regal status and ceremony. The regiment Dudley had commanded later went to Egypt and served alongside the ANZACs after he had been seconded away, costing him a possible chance to repair his standing with Australians. Better political restraint could delay the order while leaving the fleet-unit plan intact.

evidence.note: Dudley's political friction, emphasis on status, difficult relationship with Andrew Fisher, and missed chance to serve alongside the ANZACs are described.

segments.summary: Dudley's partisan friction and fondness for vice-regal ceremony give Australian political leaders a plausible way to slow the 1909 order.

segments.title: Lady Dudley's nursing work and its uncertain institutional legacy
segments.body: Lady Dudley founded a nursing organization in Australia, although her husband's prominence overshadowed her work. There may be historical connections to later outback health services. The organization's original name and the succession of later institutions remain uncertain in this account. Rebranding and competing organizational histories frustrated the attempt to trace those connections, even after consulting three books.

evidence.note: Dudley's wife is credited with founding a nursing organization. Possible links to outback health services are tentative, and the original name and later institutional succession remain unresolved after consultation of three books.

segments.summary: Lady Dudley's Australian nursing work receives brief attention, with uncertainty preserved about its original name and links to later health services.

segments.title: Why the Indefatigable class had no strong Washington case
segments.body: The historical ships were ordered while the more capable Lion class was already emerging. Much of the overseas infrastructure expense would have been incurred for either design, weakening the economy argument for the smaller ships. Their 12-inch guns and older design also left them behind the newer ships Britain could retain at Washington. Speed offered an escape from slower battleships, but enemy battlecruisers could still force them into combat. Protection and subdivision therefore mattered even without battleship-level armour, and the Indefatigables offered too little margin for damage. Jutland damaged their reputation, although their employment was also a command and doctrinal failure. British battlecruisers were intended to manoeuvre outside the battle line, while Queen Elizabeth-class battleships could sustain the prolonged exchange of heavy fire. Putting commerce-protection ships into a line that restricted evasive manoeuvres exposed them to a task they were poorly suited to perform.

evidence.note: The Indefatigables' 12-inch guns and limited protection and subdivision left them weaker than the Lion class in gunnery and survivability.
Their Jutland reputation, doctrinal misuse, and lack of treaty-era retention value are assessed.

segments.summary: The Indefatigables' 12-inch guns, limited survivability, older design, and damaged reputation leave Australia and New Zealand with little worth defending at Washington.

segments.title: Delay the orders and build 15-inch-gun Tigers
segments.body: The alternate path requires Dudley to slow down or Australian ministers to exercise more control over the timetable. Once Tiger and the Queen Elizabeth class were shaping British construction, returning to the older Indefatigable design would make little sense. The proposed ships are enlarged Tigers with eight 15-inch guns and somewhat better protection, one each for Australia, New Zealand, and the Royal Navy. Scaling from earlier increases in gun calibre gives an estimated standard displacement of roughly 31,000 tons. Reworking a familiar design keeps the proposal more conservative than starting from a wholly new concept, although the ships would still cost more than the historical Indefatigables. The scenario calls this trio the Hood class. Hood names the British 15-inch Tiger derivative, while Rodney names the ship occupying the place of the historical HMS Hood. Australia and New Zealand would ultimately operate their respective ships.

evidence.note: A procurement delay leads to three enlarged Tiger-derived battlecruisers with 15-inch guns, improved protection, and a relatively conservative design.
Scaling from earlier gun-calibre increases gives a rough estimate of 31,000 tons standard displacement.
Hood names the British 15-inch Tiger derivative, Rodney names the counterpart of historical Hood, and the two Dominion ships pass to Australia and New Zealand to operate.
The retained alternate battlecruisers are described with eight 15-inch guns and a speed of roughly 28 knots.

segments.summary: A slower Australian decision moves construction from the Indefatigable era to an enlarged Tiger design armed with 15-inch guns.

segments.title: The new battlecruisers could arrive in time for Jutland
segments.body: Ships ordered alongside the Queen Elizabeth programme would probably miss Dogger Bank and reach service before Jutland. With Queen Elizabeth-class fire control, three modern 15-inch-gun ships would join Tiger, Lion, Princess Royal, Queen Mary, and the surviving 12-inch types in a much stronger fast wing. Their arrival could leave the Queen Elizabeths with the Grand Fleet and move older battlecruisers to training or less decisive duties. Credible performance at Jutland would later give politicians a concrete wartime reason to retain fast capital ships.

evidence.note: The three 15-inch-gun ships are expected before Jutland but probably after Dogger Bank, changing Grand Fleet assignments.
Queen Elizabeth-class fire control and the proposed mix of 15-inch, 13.5-inch, and 12-inch battlecruisers are set out.

segments.summary: Three 15-inch-gun battlecruisers could enter service after Dogger Bank but before Jutland, reshaping the Grand Fleet's fast wing and wartime building choices.

segments.title: Battlecruiser orders could preserve the battleship programme
segments.body: The alternate orders could preserve all eight Revenge-class and six Queen Elizabeth-class battleships. Fisher historically argued for pausing battleship construction while pursuing the large light cruisers Courageous, Glorious, and Furious. The claim that cancellations would preserve repair space does not fit hulls already occupying slipways, which were separate from the dock facilities used for repair. In this timeline, three enlarged Tiger-derived ships already satisfy much of Fisher's demand for fast, heavy-gun vessels. Their presence makes it harder to sacrifice conventional battleships for another specialized battlecruiser programme.

evidence.note: Existing 15-inch-gun battlecruiser construction is linked to preserving the Revenge and Queen Elizabeth programmes and reducing the case for Fisher's large light cruisers.

segments.summary: Three large 15-inch-gun battlecruisers already under construction could weaken Fisher's case for cancelling battleships to free resources for Courageous, Glorious, and Furious.

segments.title: Wartime performance would make battlecruiser retention credible
segments.body: Modern 15-inch-gun ships might keep David Beatty from moving his flag to Tiger and give the battlecruiser force a more suitable flagship. Without the historical HMAS Australia available at the outbreak of war, von Spee could instead turn toward Australia. In this scenario, his raiding aims to inflict damage because the British blockade makes reaching home impractical. Japanese Kongo-class ships sent south might intercept and sink his squadron. A stronger Jutland result, paired with Tiger's record at Dogger Bank, would support both fleet scouting and commerce protection. Carriers carrying scout aircraft would also contribute to commerce protection. This wartime record would provide the political basis for seeking treaty retention.

evidence.note: The alternate wartime record combines Dogger Bank, Jutland, von Spee, and commerce protection into a retention case.

segments.summary: Better results at Jutland, continued value at Dogger Bank, and a possible interception of von Spee by Japanese battlecruisers would strengthen the retention case.

segments.title: A separate Washington category could preserve battlecruisers
segments.body: The central diplomatic change would replace Washington's single capital-ship framework with separate battleship and battlecruiser categories. Britain and Japan could invoke trade protection, while the United States could accept the category because its Lexingtons were already under construction. The proposed ship limits are 40,000 tons for battlecruisers, 35,000 tons for battleships, and 27,000 tons for aircraft carriers, with parallel 5:5:3:2:2 battlecruiser and carrier allocations. Separate entitlements for Canada, South Africa, India, Australia, and New Zealand would formalize the prewar fleet-unit concept around local sea-lane defence. Negotiations would remain difficult because the United States could demand parity with the combined British and Dominion total. Reducing each Dominion entitlement to three-quarters of a full unit is one suggested compromise, although the worked scenario retains a full unit to simplify the arithmetic. These figures are bargaining assumptions within the scenario.

evidence.note: Separate categories, ship tonnage limits, 5:5:3:2:2 allocations, named Dominion entitlements, and a possible three-quarter Dominion allowance are proposed.

segments.summary: Retention requires separate treaty categories for battleships, battlecruisers, and aircraft carriers, with fast capital ships justified by their trade-protection role.

segments.title: Dominion ships could replace some alliance reassurance
segments.body: The Dominion tonnage need not all be built immediately, and Canada could leave an allocation unused without transferring it to the Royal Navy. In the scenario, Canada also helps negotiate the end of the Anglo-Japanese Alliance. The same bargain lets Australia and New Zealand retain a tangible security guarantee as the alliance ends. Their 15-inch-gun ships would remain prestigious and militarily useful even if they ranked below treaty battleships. Local ownership ties regional reassurance directly to the treaty settlement.

evidence.note: Dominion allocations and the reassurance provided to Australia and New Zealand after the alliance are discussed.

segments.summary: Keeping modern battlecruisers could give Australia and New Zealand a visible security guarantee as the Anglo-Japanese Alliance ends.

segments.title: A separate Kongo allowance could fund more Nagatos
segments.body: Under the proposed treaty, reclassifying the four 27,500-ton Kongos would remove roughly 110,000 tons from Japan's battleship total and place it inside a 120,000-ton battlecruiser allowance. Japan could keep all four fast ships, leaving 10,000 tons unused, or replace them with three ships at the proposed 40,000-ton maximum. Retaining the Kongos preserves an extra hull in that category. The released battleship tonnage would create room for three improved Nagato-type ships. Washington would become a managed opportunity for Japanese construction as well as a limit on overall strength.

evidence.note: The Kongo tonnage moves into the battlecruiser category and frees battleship allowance for improved Nagato-type construction.

segments.summary: Moving four Kongo-class ships into a separate battlecruiser allowance would release enough Japanese battleship tonnage for three improved Nagato-type ships.

segments.title: Five Lexingtons would create an American fast wing
segments.body: The American battle line is already full, but five completed Lexington-class battlecruisers would supply the fast wing central to US scouting doctrine. Congress might dislike the expense yet still accept the ships as part of the treaty bargain, while using their existence to reject later requests for 8-inch-gun cruisers. Converting only the sixth Lexington leaves the Navy with one fast carrier and may force a slower battleship hull into a second carrier conversion. Japan could face a similar battlecruiser-and-battleship conversion pattern after earthquake damage, making carrier speed a new operational constraint for both navies.

evidence.note: Five Lexington battlecruisers, one fast carrier conversion, possible battleship-hull conversion, and the resulting scouting-force tradeoffs are discussed.

segments.summary: Completing five Lexington-class battlecruisers would give the US Navy the fast scouting force it wanted, while leaving only one fast hull available for carrier conversion.

segments.title: Speed could define a separate treaty battlecruiser category
segments.body: France has viable battlecruiser designs to consider, while Italy already has four fast Francesco Caracciolo-class hulls on the slips. Their eight 15-inch guns and projected 28-knot speed make at least two plausible candidates for completion inside a 40,000-ton battlecruiser limit. Under the proposed rule, a battlecruiser must make at least 28 knots, while a battleship can make any speed but must remain under 35,000 tons. Performance and tonnage would define the category instead of a navy's chosen label.

evidence.note: French design options, Italian Caracciolo completions, and a 28-knot performance boundary for treaty battlecruisers are proposed.

segments.summary: A proposed 28-knot minimum and 40,000-ton ceiling would let France consider dedicated designs and Italy classify fast Francesco Caracciolo-class ships as battlecruisers.

segments.title: Scheduled construction could expand Dominion fleets
segments.body: Britain, Japan, and several Dominions would enter the agreement with unused tonnage, making a timed construction programme more workable than an absolute holiday. Shipbuilding slots could limit how many ships were under construction at once and require completion within an agreed period. Britain could build ships in pairs while Japan adds battleships one at a time, and the United States could complete its Lexingtons rapidly. An Indian battlecruiser could be framed as recognition of wartime service and would provide British yards with another order. A South African battlecruiser would demand a commitment well beyond its historical naval programme. Royal Navy personnel might help crew ships flagged, owned, and funded by New Zealand or South Africa. Canada is the most likely to defer its entitlement until Pacific security concerns intensify in the late 1920s or 1930s.

evidence.note: Scheduled construction and the different Indian, South African, New Zealand, and Canadian cases.

segments.summary: Because several signatories would begin below their allowances, the alternative Washington settlement could use timed construction slots in place of a simple building holiday.

segments.title: Britain still needs County-class cruisers
segments.body: The revised capital-ship settlement would feed into a very different London Naval Treaty because the United States might enter the late 1920s with few heavy cruisers. Congress could point to the Lexingtons as powerful scouts and defer the Navy's request for Northampton-class 8-inch-gun cruisers. Britain would still build County-class cruisers because its postwar force had to cover global economic warfare, trade security, and an estimated requirement for roughly seventy cruisers. Battlecruisers and Dominion fleet units also need cruisers in their supporting squadrons, so American delay does not remove the Royal Navy's underlying requirement.

evidence.note: Lexington construction could give Congress a reason to deny requests for Northampton-class 8-inch-gun cruisers.
Delayed American heavy-cruiser construction is contrasted with Britain's global cruiser and economic-security requirements.

segments.summary: Lexington battlecruisers may postpone American heavy cruisers, but Britain's global trade-protection and fleet-screening needs still drive County-class construction.

segments.title: Lexington-carrier pairs could create early fast task forces
segments.body: A fast Lexington-class carrier could operate with one of its battlecruiser sisters as the core of an early American task force. The battlecruiser's 16-inch guns remove much of the rationale for mounting 8-inch guns on the carrier itself. Yorktown-class development could then grow around this fast formation, while a slower battleship-hull carrier supports the battle line. Giving the converted ships names such as United States or Washington would also attach unusual national prestige to naval aviation and make them especially prominent targets in any Pacific war.

evidence.note: A fast Lexington carrier-battlecruiser pairing, a slower battle-line carrier, Yorktown development, and carrier naming effects are explored.

segments.summary: Pairing a Lexington battlecruiser with the surviving fast carrier could encourage a combined aviation-and-capital-ship doctrine before later Yorktown-class development.

segments.title: Britain could divide its allowance among three battlecruisers
segments.body: British planners would have about 99,300 tons of unused battlecruiser allowance under the proposed system. Three vessels of 33,100 tons would use that allocation exactly. Two ships at the 40,000-ton ceiling would leave 19,300 tons, although the spoken calculation gives an inconsistent remainder of roughly 13,300 tons. The three-ship option therefore avoids leaving a substantial allowance unused. The ships would probably resemble the F3 concept and retain 15-inch guns. The separate 154,000-ton battleship allowance would accommodate four 35,000-ton ships, using 140,000 tons, with 16-inch guns anticipated. Those additions would leave the Royal Navy with six battlecruisers and eighteen battleships.

evidence.note: F3-like designs, the 99,300-ton allowance, three 33,100-ton battlecruisers, and four 35,000-ton battleships with 16-inch guns are proposed. The spoken 13,300-ton remainder for two maximum-size battlecruisers is inconsistent with 99,300 minus 80,000, which equals 19,300.

segments.summary: In the proposed settlement, three 33,100-ton F3-like battlecruisers would use Britain's full 99,300-ton allowance.

segments.title: Different fast wings could preserve Anglo-American parity
segments.body: The alternative settlement leaves the American and British core fleets near numerical parity while giving them different fast-wing structures. The United States has eighteen battleships and five maximum-size 40,000-ton Lexington-class battlecruisers. Britain has eighteen battleships and six smaller battlecruisers, while separate Dominion allocations expand the empire-wide total without putting every hull directly into the Royal Navy. A few French battlecruisers could also become prestige flagships, adding status competition to the fleet arithmetic.

evidence.note: Comparison of eighteen-battleship British and American fleets, their differently sized battlecruiser forces, Dominion totals, and possible French prestige ships.

segments.summary: The proposed treaty would leave Britain and the United States with eighteen battleships each, while their fast wings differ in ship size, numbers, and the place of Dominion forces.

segments.title: Italy could favour new construction over reconstruction
segments.body: Italy's usable ship count depends on how the Francesco Caracciolo class is measured against an 80,000-ton allowance. An aggressive claim of roughly 26,000 tons standard displacement might squeeze in three ships, although their loading makes that figure doubtful. Even a smaller completion programme gives Italy a substantially stronger fast battle line. With treaty-approved construction available, later funds are more likely to go toward new ships than extensive reconstructions of older battleships.

evidence.note: Italian tonnage claims, possible Caracciolo completions, cost, and the shift from rebuilding old battleships to new construction are assessed.

segments.summary: Treaty permission to finish Francesco Caracciolo-class ships could give Italy a modern fast battle line and reduce the appeal of rebuilding older battleships.

segments.title: French and Dutch commerce protection could support battlecruisers
segments.body: France could use fast capital ships as the centre of a third major formation alongside its Mediterranean and Atlantic forces. Their likely purpose would be overseas imperial policing and commerce protection in the Far East. Once the treaty formally recognizes that mission, the Netherlands could also decide to acquire a battlecruiser in the 1920s. Dutch options include a British or French design, purchase of the fourth Francesco Caracciolo hull from Italy, or domestic construction. Any of these choices would extend the category beyond the original signatories' main fleets.

evidence.note: French overseas fleet roles and a possible Dutch commerce-protection battlecruiser for the East Indies are proposed.

segments.summary: French battlecruisers could form an overseas imperial-policing force, while the Netherlands might buy a foreign design, acquire an Italian hull, or build its own ship.

segments.title: New battleships could give Japan a treaty success
segments.body: Japan would still receive a 3:5 relationship instead of the 7:10 ratio many advocates wanted. The revised settlement would also permit new battleships, giving the navy a concrete achievement to claim from the conference. Those ships would offer visible status and a focus for naval pride, which could make the treaty appear less purely restrictive. The interpretation connects Japan's perceived insecurity with some of its later decisions, while explicitly distinguishing explanation from an excuse for aggression. Examining the reasoning behind harmful choices can help identify the assumptions and fears that led people toward them. In this scenario, greater confidence from the new ships could change those calculations.

evidence.note: New treaty construction is connected to Japanese naval pride, international status, confidence, and later strategic decision-making.

segments.summary: Although Japan would still accept an inferior ratio, permission to build new battleships could give the navy a concrete achievement around which to rally status and confidence.

segments.title: Dominion capital ships would demand local naval infrastructure
segments.body: With their own capital ships, Australia and New Zealand would rely less on distant imperial forces for reassurance. The ships would become a focus for modernization and growth in each Dominion navy. Expanding the navies to support them would be difficult and would require sustained infrastructure investment throughout the 1920s and 1930s. If the Second World War still developed as it did historically, that preparation would leave both navies materially different from their historical counterparts.

evidence.note: Dominion ownership, confidence, naval growth, and the infrastructure investment needed before a possible 1939 war are linked.

segments.summary: Retained battlecruisers would give Australia and New Zealand a fleet cornerstone, with a difficult commitment to naval growth and supporting infrastructure.

segments.title: More fast capital ships could disrupt German rearmament
segments.body: Germany would confront larger British, American, French, Italian, and Japanese fleets before beginning its own rearmament. Numerous fast capital ships make the Deutschland-class commerce-raider concept far less attractive, because even France can deploy ships capable of hunting them. If Germany does not build the Deutschlands, it may also lack the industrial progression needed to produce the Scharnhorst class and then the Bismarck class on the historical timetable. The same altered balance could push the Soviet Union toward capital ships earlier, making the familiar naval setting of the Second World War increasingly unlikely.

evidence.note: Larger treaty fleets are linked to the viability of the Deutschland, Scharnhorst, and Bismarck programmes and to earlier Soviet capital-ship ambitions.

segments.summary: A world crowded with battlecruisers could weaken the German commerce-raider strategy and redirect both German and Soviet capital-ship programmes.

segments.title: Dominion carriers could accelerate naval aviation
segments.body: If aircraft carriers share the commerce-protection justification used for battlecruisers, each Dominion could receive an entitlement to one carrier of up to 27,000 tons. Governments might use that allowance for one large armoured carrier. Choosing two improved Hermes-sized ships of roughly 13,000 tons each would require a creative interpretation of the nominal one-carrier limit. The scenario imagines ten such ships around the world by 1939, comparable in size to light fleet carriers. With smaller carriers distributed around the empire, the Royal Navy would have more reason to concentrate on large fleet carriers. Individual fleets could also seek Unicorn-type forward aviation support ships, raising the question of where carrier support ends and an additional carrier begins. More participating navies would broaden practical experience in naval aviation, bombing, and aircraft development. The scenario still depends on modern 15-inch-gun battlecruisers proving enough wartime value to make treaty retention credible.

evidence.note: The transcript explores Dominion carrier allowances, improved Hermes-sized ships, larger Royal Navy carriers, and aviation support vessels.
The conclusion restates that proven wartime value and 15-inch-gun ships are necessary for treaty retention.

segments.summary: A Dominion entitlement to one 27,000-ton carrier could support a large ship, while pairs of improved Hermes-sized ships depend on interpreting that one-ship restriction creatively.
